title: Writing an Office Cleaning RFP Template That Eliminates Hidden Fees
seoTitle: Office Cleaning RFP Template Guide to Eliminate Hidden Fees
metaDescription: Build an office cleaning RFP template that locks in $0.05-$0.20/sq ft base rates, 4.33-week billing math, and periodic floor schedules. Compare bids online.
excerpt: Download-ready architectural blueprint for structuring a commercial office cleaning Request for Proposal (RFP) that forces every bidding contractor onto identical pricing and labor lines. Learn how to define cleanable square footage by surface type, lock in 4.33-week frequency math, and separate base janitorial labor from periodic restoration.
quickAnswer: An effective commercial office cleaning rfp template mandates that every bidder price the exact same net cleanable square footage across a 4.33-week monthly calendar, disclose committed nightly labor hours benchmarked against 3,500 sq ft/hr ($35 to $65/hr standard bill rate), and itemize base cleaning ($0.05 to $0.20/sq ft by building size) separately from restrooms ($15 to $30/visit), consumables ($0.012 to $0.025/sq ft/visit), and amortized quarterly floor care ($0.03 to $0.06/sq ft/month).

blocks.text: Why Generic 1-Page Bid Requests Produce Incomparable Janitorial Quotes

When a facility manager emails three commercial cleaning companies a casual request asking for 'a quote to clean our 18,000-square-foot office three nights a week,' each contractor writes their own rules. One bidder prices the full 18,000 gross leased square feet including locked IT closets and unfinished warehouse bays; the second bidder subtracts 2,800 square feet of non-cleanable zones; and the third bidder submits an ultra-low base retainer while burying appliance cleaning, interior glass, and high-dusting inside a 'time-and-materials extra at $75/hr' addendum.

A well-engineered office cleaning rfp template removes contractor guesswork by dictating the exact bid submission worksheet, facility profile data, task frequency matrix, and mandatory compliance attachments. When you control the bid worksheet structure, every vendor must fill in the same mathematical cells—allowing you to audit their production rates, hourly wage assumptions, and add-on unit costs in minutes.

blocks.title: Mandate an Excel or Structured Bid Sheet Attachment
blocks.text: State explicitly in Section 1 of your RFP template that proposals submitted solely on vendor marketing letterhead without completing your standardized Pricing & Labor Breakdown Schedule (Exhibit B) will be rejected as non-responsive.
Core Sections of a Commercial Janitorial RFP Template & Pricing Schedule

Your commercial janitorial rfp template should be organized into six binding sections, culminating in the standardized Bid Pricing Schedule shown in the table below. Requiring bidders to populate each row separately prevents cross-subsidization and exposes hidden fees before contract execution.

blocks.caption: Standardized RFP Exhibit B: Mandatory Bid Pricing & Labor Breakdown Schedule
rows: Line 1: Net Cleanable Base Facility Care
Nightly labor hours + effective $/hr rate + $/sq ft/visit
$0.05-$0.20/sq ft by bracket; $35-$65/hr; 3,500 sq ft/hr pace
Verifies adequate daily staffing for trash, dusting, and vacuuming/mopping.
Line 2: Restroom Sanitization & Descaling
Fixture count + dedicated minutes/night + cost per restroom/visit
$15-$30 per restroom per visit (15-25 mins per multi-stall room)
Ensures hospital-grade dwell time on fixtures, partitions, and floor drains.
Line 3: Breakroom & Kitchenette Package
Daily sink, counter, microwave interior/exterior & fridge wipe-down
$12-$25 per breakroom per visit
Prevents extra work-order billing for microwave splatters and coffee sinks.
Line 4: Interior Glass & Conference Partitions
Entry doors, sidelights, and full-height glass conference walls
$15-$35 per visit (or scheduled weekly/biweekly detail)
Eliminates ambiguity between 'entry door glass' and interior office glass.
Line 5: Consumables Restocking Allowance
Paper towels, 2-ply bath tissue, foam soap, and can liners
$0.012-$0.025/sq ft/visit (or open-book wholesale case price list)
Caps vendor handling markups and locks in exact roll footage and liner mil specs.
Line 6: Quarterly Deep Floor Care (Amortized)
Hot-water carpet extraction + VCT machine scrub-and-recoat
$0.03-$0.06/sq ft/month amortized ($55-$95/hr specialty labor)
Guarantees 4 scheduled weekend restoration visits per year without surprise quotes.
Line 7: Total Monthly Fixed Retainer (4.33 Wks/Mo)
Sum of Lines 1-6 multiplied by exact monthly visit count
Locks in 12 equal monthly invoices with zero 5th-week billing surprises.

blocks.text: How to Specify Flooring Surfaces, Headcount, and Frequency Multipliers in Section 2

Bidders cannot calculate accurate labor hours unless Section 2 (Facility Profile) of your rfp template breaks down your total cleanable square footage by exact flooring material and occupancy density. Different surfaces carry distinct labor multipliers against the baseline 1.00x commercial carpet tile rate:

items: Commercial Carpet & Carpet Tiles (1.00x Multiplier): Specify whether high-traffic corridors require CRI Seal of Approval HEPA backpack vacuums and immediate enzymatic spot extraction.
VCT / LVT Vinyl Plank (1.04x Multiplier): Require neutral-pH damp mopping nightly plus scheduled high-speed burnishing or scrub-and-recoat maintenance.

Mixed Carpet + Hard Floors (1.05x Multiplier): Note the percentage split (for example, 70% carpet tile / 30% LVT) because crews must stage both dry vacuuming and wet microfiber mopping setups every visit.
Engineered / Solid Hardwood (1.08x Multiplier): Mandate low-moisture flat microfiber pads and wood-safe neutral cleaners; prohibit string mops and standing water.
Ceramic Tile & Grout (1.12x Multiplier): Account for 12% higher floor labor due to rotary grout-line scrubbing and alkaline degreaser dwell time in restrooms and lobbies.
Polished Concrete (0.95x Multiplier): Note elevator doorway width if the vendor can deploy a compact walk-behind auto-scrubber to capture the 5% labor efficiency gain.

blocks.text: Equally important, specify your exact service frequency and size tier so bidders understand your expected price corridor. Suites under 2,500 square feet benchmark at $0.12 to $0.20 per square foot (or a $90 to $135 per-visit minimum); 2,500 to 9,999 square feet runs $0.09 to $0.15 per square foot; 10,000 to 24,999 square feet runs $0.07 to $0.12 per square foot; and 25,000+ square feet runs $0.05 to $0.10 per square foot. If you request alternative frequency pricing in your RFP—for instance, comparing 2x/week (1.00x multiplier, 8.66 visits/month) against 3x/week (0.95x multiplier, 13.0 visits/month) or 5x/week (0.90x multiplier, 21.65 visits/month)—require bidders to complete separate Exhibit B columns for each option.
Standardizing Waste Stream Hardware and Closet Infrastructure in the RFP

Section 3 of your office cleaning rfp template should inventory your building's waste and recycling receptacles alongside your janitorial closet dimensions. Centralizing trash collection into properly vented commercial containers reduces nightly collection labor by up to 20% and prevents liner tears across carpeted corridors.

Specify in your facility inventory whether your janitorial closet and freight dock are equipped with heavy-duty mobile barrels like the Rubbermaid Commercial Brute 44-Gallon Vented Trash Can (crafted from NSF-listed LLDPE resin with integrated venting channels that cut liner pull force by 50%), or require the winning contractor to furnish them on-site. In copy hubs, mailrooms, and breakroom pantries, listing standardized narrow-footprint stations such as the 11-inch-wide Rubbermaid Commercial Slim Jim 23-Gallon Recycling & Waste Station with molded bag cinches ensures bidders stock the exact liner dimensions without charging oversized bag fees. For Class A main lobbies and elevator banks, note architectural receptacles such as the Safco Public Square 37-Gallon Commercial Steel Receptacle with fire-safe powder-coated steel and internal liner retainers so the RFP scope explicitly includes nightly exterior stainless/steel wipe-down and polish.
6-Step Timeline for Running a Competitive Commercial Cleaning RFP

items.name: Week 1: Finalize Net Cleanable Floor Plans and Fixture Counts
items.text: Mark up a PDF floor plan shading cleanable carpet, hard floor, restroom, and breakroom zones, and count every toilet, urinal, sink, paper towel dispenser, and waste receptacle.

items.name: Week 2: Issue the RFP Package to 3 to 5 Pre-Qualified Bidders
items.text: Send the RFP template and Exhibit B spreadsheet only to commercial contractors carrying verified W-2 staffing, active local office portfolios, and $1M/$2M General Liability coverage.

items.name: Week 3: Host a Mandatory Guided Site Walkthrough
items.text: Walk bidders through the exact scope areas, show the water source and lockable storage in the janitorial closet, and publish a single written Q&A addendum to all participants within 48 hours.

items.name: Week 4: Audit Submitted Exhibit B Pricing Schedules
items.text: Normalize every returned spreadsheet against the 4.33-week calendar multiplier, ISSA 3,500 sq ft/hr labor pace, and $35-$65/hr standard hourly rate corridor.

items.name: Week 5: Conduct Finalist Operations Interviews and Reference Checks
items.text: Interview the designated Account Manager and night supervisor for your top two or three scorers and verify three active local references of similar square footage.

items.name: Week 6: Execute the Service Level Agreement and 30-Day Mobilization Plan
items.text: Attach your RFP Scope Matrix and Exhibit B labor hours as binding contract exhibits, collect live COI endorsements, and issue security keycards for supervised onboarding shifts.

blocks.title: Mandatory RFP Compliance Clauses (COI, OSHA & Security)
blocks.text: Include a non-negotiable compliance checklist in Section 5 of your RFP template: (1) Certificate of Insurance naming Building Owner and Tenant as Additional Insured ($1M/$2M General Liability, $1M Auto, Statutory Workers' Comp, $50k Janitorial Dishonesty Bond); (2) OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 HazCom SDS binder and Bloodborne Pathogen spill procedures; and (3) 7-year criminal background check verification for every assigned badge holder.

Building your RFP pricing baseline? Run your facility square footage, flooring mix, and restroom count through our Office Cleaning Cost Calculator & Quote Comparator to establish your target budget before sending out bid packets.

faqs.q: How many vendors should I invite when issuing an office cleaning RFP?
faqs.a: Invite three to five pre-qualified commercial building service contractors. Three complete, responsive proposals provide sufficient market competition to benchmark labor hours and hourly bill rates ($35 to $65/hr), while keeping mandatory site walkthroughs and reference verifications manageable for your facilities team.

faqs.q: Should all bidders walk the facility together or in separate appointments?
faqs.a: Separate 30-to-45-minute walkthrough appointments on the same day work best for commercial offices, provided every bidder receives the exact same written RFP packet and all questions asked during any tour are compiled into a single anonymized Q&A addendum emailed to every participant.

faqs.q: How do I prevent contractors from underbidding the RFP and cutting hours later?
faqs.a: Require bidders to state committed nightly labor hours and weekly supervisor audit hours in Exhibit B of your RFP template, and incorporate Exhibit B into the final contract with a clause allowing pro-rata invoice deductions whenever electronic geofenced timekeeping logs fall more than 5% below contracted hours.

faqs.q: What is the difference between daily periodic tasks and quarterly restorative tasks in an RFP?
faqs.a: Daily and weekly tasks (trash removal, restroom disinfection, HEPA vacuuming, damp mopping, breakroom wipe-downs) belong in your base monthly retainer. Restorative tasks like hot-water carpet extraction and VCT strip/scrub-and-recoat should be specified on a separate amortized quarterly floor care line ($0.03 to $0.06/sq ft/month) tied to fixed calendar weekends.
